explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Asaph says, "They did not remember His power…" and the verse goes right on to the day He redeemed them from the adversary. I lose my oven mitts three times a week, so I get forgetting small things. But forgetting a rescue like that? That's a big one to let slip.
No road back to Egypt shows up in this verse. Asaph says they did not remember His power, the day He redeemed them from the adversary. Nobody needed a map when the real trouble was a short memory.

Their fathers do come up later in this psalm, but not here. What Asaph says they did not remember was His power, the day He redeemed them from the adversary. Names are easy to hold onto. A rescue is the thing worth remembering.

Not quite, friend. Asaph says God turned their rivers to blood, "and from their streams they could not drink." So the water was no good for drinking. I can't even picture mixing a batch of dough with that.

Right, it's false. The verse says He turned their rivers to blood, "and from their streams they could not drink." The very water they counted on was gone. If my well did that, I'd close the bakery for the day and sit down.

Yes, baker. Asaph says, "He killed their vines with hailstones and their sycamore-figs with sleet." Then He "abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning." Fields and herds both got hit, and the weather did the work.

Ships and harbors never come up in these verses. The hail struck their vines and their cattle, and the sleet hit their sycamore-figs. This part of the song stays out in the fields and pastures. Nobody here is anywhere near a dock.

Temples and idols aren't named in these verses. Asaph says the hail killed their vines, and He abandoned their cattle to the hail. The sleet came down on their sycamore-figs. It's all crops and livestock in this stretch.

That's the one, friend. Asaph says, "He led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness." I love the picture. A flock follows its shepherd, and the shepherd does the leading.

No ranks and no marching orders in this verse. Asaph says God led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock. I'd say that's a gentler picture than soldiers. A flock stays close to the one leading it.
No chariots here, baker. The verse says He led them like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness. A parade of sheep doesn't look like much, but that's the picture Asaph picked.
True. Asaph says, "He led them safely, so they did not fear…" Safe, so no fear. I get jumpy on a stepladder, so I'm impressed. Their safety came from the One leading them.
Not this time, friend. The verse says, "He led them safely, so they did not fear…" That makes the statement true. They were led safely, and that's why they did not fear.

Yes! Asaph says, "…but the sea engulfed their enemies." God's people went through safely and the enemies did not. It's the same sea Asaph sang about earlier in this psalm, when God split it (Psalm 78:13).
No peace talks in this verse, baker. Asaph says the sea engulfed their enemies. No handshakes and no treaty. Just the sea.
That isn't what the verse says. It says God led His people safely, "but the sea engulfed their enemies." Nobody gets a trip back. The sea is what settles it.

Yes, inheritance. Asaph says God "drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance; He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents." Apportioned means divided up. Picture a big pan of cookies cut so every tribe gets a piece.
Armies don't show up in this verse, friend. God drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance. The tribes were settled in their tents. This is a verse about homes, not battles.

Kings aren't in this verse. Asaph says God drove out nations before Israel and apportioned their inheritance. Then He settled the tribes in their tents. A king isn't handed out here, but a place to live is.

True. Asaph says, "They turned back and were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow." That echoes the start of this psalm, where he hoped the children wouldn't be stubborn like their fathers (Psalm 78:8). I think that's why this line stings.
It's true, friend. Asaph says, "They turned back and were faithless like their fathers…" The tribes did the very thing the earlier verses warned about. That makes the statement true.

Idols, baker. Asaph says, "They enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols." High places and idols are the two things he names in this verse. Both of them stirred up God's anger.
Horses never come up here, friend. The verse says they provoked His jealousy with their idols. Their high places enraged Him too. Nothing in the stable is mentioned.
No riches in this verse. Asaph says Israel enraged God with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols. The word he uses for what stirred God's jealousy is idols.

That's the one. Asaph says, "He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men." A tabernacle is a tent, and this one was where God had pitched His presence among people. It's a heavy line, so I'll let it sit.
The temple in Jerusalem isn't named in this verse. Asaph says God abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men. The word he uses is tent. Shiloh is the place.
An altar at Bethel isn't in this verse, baker. Asaph names the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men. That's the place God abandoned in this line.

Shame, friend. Asaph says, "He beat back His foes; He put them to everlasting shame." The foes get beaten back, and the shame he names is everlasting. After the heavy verses before it, this is where things turn.
Peace isn't the word, baker. The verse says He beat back His foes and put them to everlasting shame. His foes get beaten back, and shame is what lasts.
Glory isn't the word here. Asaph says the Lord beat back His foes and put them to everlasting shame. It's a good word to find in a fill in the blank, but it isn't in this verse.

Not so, friend. Asaph says God rejected the tent of Joseph and refused the tribe of Ephraim. Then comes the next verse: "But He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved." So He did choose another tribe.

Right, it's false. After rejecting Joseph's tent and Ephraim, Asaph says, "But He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved." That "But" is doing a lot of work in the verse. God chose Judah.

It's the opposite, baker. Asaph says, "He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever." He compares it to the heights and the earth, and nothing here says tent. Not something that won't last.

False is right. Asaph says, "He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever." My cookie planet is just big enough for a bakery, so a comparison to the whole earth impresses me. This sanctuary is built to last.
That's it. Asaph says, "from tending the ewes He brought him to be shepherd of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance." The job title stayed shepherd. The flock just got a lot bigger.
Priest isn't the job here, friend. The verse says God brought David from tending the ewes to be shepherd of His people Jacob. The tabernacle isn't mentioned in this verse.
No army in this verse, baker. Asaph says God brought David from tending the ewes to be shepherd of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance. The new job is shepherd.
Yes, baker. Asaph says, "So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands." The heart and the hands both get named. That's a lovely way to end a long song.
Not a heavy hand, friend. Asaph says David shepherded them with integrity of heart. He also says David guided them "with skillful hands." Skillful is the word he picked.
No trembling in this verse. Asaph says David shepherded God's people with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands. That sounds steady to me.
